summary: The measured level differences hold up within one mounting, but several of the report's strongest claims go beyond its own evidence. The worst problems: the cut-in exclusion rests on numbers that a standard model does not reproduce, and the report's own Voc data (Fig. 6c) contradict "no sign of a Reynolds-number-dependent transition" and "uniform multiplier". Other problems: the wind-offset, test-order, β and Cp(λ) arguments are overstated; the remount decision rule is statistically wrong; the tip-speed ratio (about 0.1 to 0.2, recoverable from the July EMF line) is never stated, and it reframes the whole mechanism discussion.

findings.location: Sec. 5.5 'Scaling with wind speed', p.11 (also relied on in Sec. 7 (ii), p.14)
findings.quote: shifting cut-in by 0.5 m/s changes the level by about 15% but also lowers n by about 0.27, which the data exclude.
findings.problem: Neither number can be reproduced, and they overstate how strongly the exponent excludes a cut-in or friction difference. They are typed by hand; they are not in build_report.py and are copied from docs/09 with no derivation, despite Sec. 1 saying 'every number in this report is generated from those files'. A standard cut-in model gives roughly +9.4% level and Δn ≈ −0.10 per 0.5 m/s. The exponent test therefore excludes a cut-in shift as the whole explanation only narrowly for Ra 40, and it allows a partial cut-in contribution of about 4–5 percentage points: more than half of Ra 40's +8.4% and about a third of Ra 80's gain.
findings.evidence: build/review/claims/a6.py and a7.py. P = a(v−v0)^m fitted to Ra 20 raw Pmax gives v0 = 0.83 m/s, m = 3.60. A −0.5 m/s shift gives +9.4% geometric-mean level and Δn = −0.100 (slope of the log-ratio vs ln v, the report's own Δn definition). Choosing v0 from 0 to 6 m/s with m constrained to reproduce n = 3.77 gives +9.4 to +10.1% and Δn −0.095 to −0.158; no choice gives +15% / −0.27. Scaled up to fake the full gain: Ra 40 needs Δn ≈ −0.086 against a CI of [−0.055, +0.061]; Ra 80 needs ≈ −0.136 against [−0.047, +0.095]. At the CI lower bounds, a cut-in shift of about 0.23 m/s (Ra 40) or 0.24 m/s (Ra 80) is still allowed, worth about 4–5% in level.
findings.fix: Generate the argument in build_report.py from a stated model (e.g. P = a(v−v0)^m fitted to Ra 20) and print the model. Replace the sentence with: 'In a cut-in model fitted to Ra 20, a 0.5 m/s shift changes the level by about 9% and n by about −0.10. A shift large enough to produce the whole Ra 80 gain would give Δn ≈ −0.14, outside the measured [−0.05, +0.10]; for Ra 40 the margin is small. The exponent allows a cut-in contribution of up to about 4–5% of level.' Update Sec. 7 (ii) to match.

findings.location: Sec. 7 (iii), p.14; Summary bullet 3, p.1; Sec. 5.5 'uniform multipliers'; Fig. 6c
findings.quote: There is no sign of a Reynolds-number-dependent transition. A boundary-layer mechanism of the golf-ball kind would be expected to switch on over part of the range rather than act uniformly across it.
findings.problem: The report's own rotor-speed proxy contradicts this. The report says the gain is 'carried by rotor speed' (Voc). The Ra 80 Voc advantage grows significantly with wind speed: in Fig. 6c the green line runs about 2–4% at 10–17 m/s and 7–10% at 31–38 m/s, while Ra 40 stays flat at about 4%. The claim rests only on the power-level Δn ≈ 0, a linear-in-ln v test that has little power against a change confined to part of the range. Its CI also allows the Ra 80 gain to change by −6% to +13% across the range, which is the size of the effect itself. 'Uniform multiplier' in the Summary is overstated for the same reason.
findings.evidence: build/review/claims/a5.py. Slope of ln(Voc ratio) vs ln v: Ra 80 vs Ra 40 = +0.042 ± 0.025 (p = 0.003, Spearman 0.69, p = 0.007); Ra 80 vs Ra 20 = +0.031 ± 0.031 (p = 0.051). The first-step voltage (no fitting) agrees: Ra 80 vs Ra 40 slope +0.048 ± 0.028 (p = 0.002); Ra 80 vs Ra 20 +0.040 ± 0.038 (p = 0.042). Power ratio Ra 80/Ra 20 averages +15.7% at 1600–1800 rpm against +10.9% at 500–900 and +10.6% at 1200–1500 (Fig. 1 rising tail). Δn CI for Ra 80 [−0.047, +0.095] over ln(38.0/10.2) = 1.31 allows the gain to change by −5.9% to +13.3% across the range (a1.py).
findings.fix: Delete (iii), or replace it with: 'The power ratio shows no significant linear trend with ln v, but the test is weak (the gain could change by ±10% across the range). The Ra 80 open-circuit voltage advantage does grow with wind speed (Fig. 6c; slope +0.04 per ln v, p ≈ 0.003 against Ra 40), which is what a roughness-triggered transition would produce, so this mechanism is not excluded.' In the Summary, change 'uniform multiplier' to 'no detectable change in the power-law exponent'.

findings.location: Sec. 7 last paragraph, p.15; Sec. 7 'The blade geometry matters', p.15; Table 1 / Sec. 2.1
findings.quote: is 0.09–0.27%, far below a working H-rotor, because the generator loads the rotor far down its Cp(λ) curve.
findings.problem: The report never states the tip-speed ratio, although the data package allows it to be estimated. By the July EMF calibration, the free-running tip-speed ratio is only about 0.11–0.22. At that λ the rotor works as a drag machine (a Savonius/cup-anemometer-like device with 183° buckets), not a lift-driven H-rotor. That changes how the results should be read: (a) comparing it with 'a working H-rotor' misplaces the operating regime, which is low λ even at no load; the low Cp_el is not only 'the generator loads the rotor'. (b) Airfoil and wing references (Laitone; Sandia) are the wrong reference class. (c) The relevant physics is the difference in drag between the concave and convex sides, where roughness on the convex side is a textbook drag-crisis mechanism. A wind-energy referee will ask for λ first.
findings.evidence: build/daq_july/FINDINGS.md §6: EMF line from zero-current July data, Voc = 0.03342·rpm − 0.448 V; audit2 also finds the lab zero-current voltages at 500–700 rpm (3.03/4.13/5.33 V) close to the rig's (2.85/4.47/5.62 V). Applied to the rig's Voc (Table 9), free-running rotor speed is 109–717 rpm for Ra 20 and 113–782 rpm for Ra 80. With R = 0.1016 m that is λ_free = 0.113→0.201 (Ra 20) and 0.117→0.219 (Ra 80) (a4.py). This agrees with the July Measured_RPM under load: 554 rpm at 1800 fan rpm, λ ≈ 0.155. Even allowing for the ch3 pulse ambiguity, λ cannot exceed about 0.22.
findings.fix: Add to Sec. 2.1 or 5.4: 'Using the generator EMF constant from the 27 July zero-load data (0.0334 V/rpm), the rig's Voc corresponds to free-running speeds of about 110–780 rpm, i.e. λ ≈ 0.11–0.22. Even unloaded, the rotor runs in the drag-driven regime, far below the λ ≈ 3–5 of a lift-driven H-rotor.' Rewrite Sec. 7's geometry paragraph against drag-rotor and bluff-body literature (semicircular cups or cylinders, Savonius roughness studies), and drop the 'working H-rotor' comparison or qualify it.

findings.location: Sec. 7 'Alternative explanations', Wind speed on the day, p.15; Table 7 row 'No independent wind measurement', p.16
findings.quote: by about −3.2% for the Voc change seen in Ra 80, against an observed −0.4% (CI [−2.2, +1.5]), which excludes it.
findings.problem: This only excludes a wind offset that accounts for all of the Ra 80 voltage gain, and only narrowly. A partial offset is consistent with the data: up to about two-thirds of the Ra 80 gain (roughly 9 of the 13.7 points) could be a day-to-day wind difference without contradicting Rint. The prediction also applies one global exponent (Rint ∝ v^−0.79), but Rint is nearly flat above about 30 m/s (Fig. 6b, Table 9: 36.8, 36.6, 36.2, 36.5 Ω), which is exactly where the Ra 80 Voc gain is largest. With local slopes the predicted change is −2.75%, barely outside the CI. The report's own 1000–1100 rpm 'low Ra 20 reading' shows the wind-offset signature: Ra 80 vs Ra 20 Voc is +10.5% and +9.9% while Rint is −4.9% and −5.1%, close to the −5% the scaling predicts. So effective-wind differences of several percent between runs do occur on this rig.
findings.evidence: a2.py and the follow-up script. Largest wind fraction of the Ra 80 Voc change consistent with the Rint CI lower bound (−2.19%): 0.67 with the global −0.791/1.497 scaling, 0.79 with 5-point local slopes (pooled local dlnR/dlnv runs from −0.96 mid-range to −0.25 at 33–36 m/s). Local-slope prediction for the full offset: −2.75% (Ra 80), −1.82% (Ra 40).
findings.fix: Replace 'which excludes it' with: 'which argues against a wind offset explaining all of the Ra 80 gain, but allows one explaining up to about two-thirds of it; for Ra 40 the test is uninformative.' In Table 7 change 'excluded only for Ra 80' to 'not excluded; a full-size offset is disfavoured for Ra 80 only'. Note that the 1000–1100 rpm excess carries this signature.

findings.location: Summary bullet 2, p.1; Sec. 7 'Test order and software changes', p.15
findings.quote: Ra 40, run last, sits between the other two, so a steady drift with test date cannot produce the ordering
findings.problem: The argument only excludes a monotonic drift. A step change between 20 and 26 August would lift both textured rotors above Ra 20, and that step would produce the two headline numbers. Ra 20 is the only run before PMC 3.0 and firmware v4/v5, before the 25 Aug drive-profile restore and readback change, and it was written by pre-git code. The Summary's 'although the rotors were tested in the order Ra 20, Ra 80, Ra 40' implies test order is dealt with. 'Every recomputed number agree[s] across runs' shows only that the analysis reproduces the logs, not that the measurement chain behaved the same. The report also omits a known hardware difference: a magnet was fixed to one blade for the reed switch after the Ra 80 run, so the Ra 40 rotor (the only run with rotor pulses) carried a magnet on a blade.
findings.evidence: git log 20–26 Aug (4d17ec4, 465f286, 292ca13, 67571f4 'one magnet on one blade', committed 26 Aug 15:55, after the Ra 80 run ended at 15:32). build/audit2/rig-runs_details.md: 'Confounds for Ra20 … only one before PMC 3.0/v4/v5 and the 25 Aug drive-profile restore and readback change'; 'Confound for Ra40 … a magnet was on a blade'; 'The Ra80 vs Ra40 contrast (+4.91% raw / +4.53% fit) is the cleanest.'
findings.fix: Summary: '…although tested in the order Ra 20, Ra 80, Ra 40, which rules out a steady drift but not a one-off change between the first run and the others. The comparison free of that confound, Ra 80 vs Ra 40, is +4.9% [+2.4, +7.4], higher at 13 of 14.' In Sec. 2.2 and Sec. 7, add: 'The Ra 40 rotor carried a small magnet on one blade for the reed switch; the others did not.' Delete 'every recomputed number agree across runs'.

findings.location: Sec. 9 item 1, p.16; 'Most valuable next measurement', p.1
findings.quote: The result is the mount-to-mount error bar. Below about 3% the present results stand; above about 10%, mounting dominates and every rotor needs two mountings.
findings.problem: One remount gives a single difference, a one-degree-of-freedom estimate of mount-to-mount spread, and that is not an error bar. The 95% interval for σ from one pair spans roughly 0.45× to 32× the observed value, so a small result cannot show that mounting variance is small. The 3% threshold is also wrong. With σ_m = 3%, two single mountings differ by about 4.2% (1 SD), so Ra 80 vs Ra 40 (+4.9%) and the monotonic ordering would not stand, and Ra 40 vs Ra 20 would be marginal. The report would be committing in advance to a decision rule that does not hold.
findings.evidence: A difference of single mountings has SD σ_m·√2. For a 2-SD difference: Ra 80 vs Ra 40 (ln 1.049 = 0.048) needs σ_m ≤ 1.7%; Ra 40 vs Ra 20 (0.081) needs σ_m ≤ 2.9%; Ra 80 vs Ra 20 (0.128) needs σ_m ≤ 4.5%. For 1 dof, CI for σ = s·[1/√χ²(0.975,1), 1/√χ²(0.025,1)] = s·[0.45, 31.9].
findings.fix: Replace with: 'A single remount of Ra 20 detects a large mounting effect but cannot show that it is small. If it moves Pmax by more than about 3%, the Ra 40 vs Ra 20 and Ra 80 vs Ra 40 differences are not established. Establishing them needs at least two remounts of each rotor in randomised order; the ordering requires mount-to-mount SD below about 1.5–2%.'

findings.location: Summary bullet 2, p.1; Sec. 5.3, p.9; Fig. 5
findings.quote: Pmax ∝ tfuzz^0.092 (95% CI 0.075–0.109), about +6.6% per doubling of fuzzy-skin thickness … so if anything the gain is front-loaded.
findings.problem: The β interval is pseudo-replicated. It treats 42 (rotor, set point) values as independent, with 27 residual dof, although texture varies across only three rotors, each mounted once. Any error shared by a whole run (mounting, day, print) enters β fully and is absent from the CI. A plausible ±3% offset on the single Ra 20 mounting moves β from 0.071 to 0.114, beyond both ends of the quoted CI. 'Front-loaded' is not significant even within a mounting, and a −3.2% Ra 20 offset removes it. The bullet's later general caveat ('the intervals above describe scatter across wind speeds…') does not undo the impression a CI on a dose–response exponent gives.
findings.evidence: a5.py. Rotor-level regression of the three mean ln Pmax on ln t: β = 0.092, 95% half-width 0.168 (1 dof). Ra 20 offsets of −5/−3/+3/+5% give β = 0.129/0.114/0.071/0.057. Step1 − step2 = 2lnP40 − lnP20 − lnP80: mean 0.033, CI [−0.004, +0.070]; Ra 20 offset that equalises the steps: −3.2%. At 1600–1800 rpm the two steps are +8.0% and +7.2% (not front-loaded).
findings.fix: Remove the CI on β from the Summary, or label it: 'about +6.6% per doubling (three rotors, one mounting each; no uncertainty can yet be attached)'. In Sec. 5.3 delete 'so if anything the gain is front-loaded', or add that the curvature is not significant and disappears with a 3% Ra 20 mounting offset.

findings.location: Sec. 3.4, p.7; Summary bullet 1; Fig. 1; Table 4; Sec. 5.2 ('the mean over 14 set points is far tighter')
findings.quote: with a 95% confidence interval from the t distribution on the log-ratios (13 degrees of freedom). This interval measures how consistently the difference holds across wind speeds within one mounting
findings.problem: Even as a within-mounting measure, the t-interval assumes 14 independent, exchangeable set points. The Ra 80/Ra 20 log-ratios are serially correlated (the 1000–1100 rpm bump, the rising tail), so that interval is too narrow. The '14 of 14' and '13 of 14' counts are also used as if the set points were independent replications, but a single mounting offset would produce 14/14 on its own. The sign test is defined in Sec. 3.4 but never reported.
findings.evidence: a1.py and a5.py. Lag-1 autocorrelation of the log-ratios: Ra 80/Ra 20 0.52 (0.51 detrended), Ra 40/Ra 20 0.14, Ra 80/Ra 40 0.28. An AR(1) effective-n correction (n_eff ≈ 4.5) widens Ra 80 vs Ra 20 from [+10.7, +16.9]% to about [+6.5, +21.5]%; Ra 40 vs Ra 20 [+6.1, +10.8] to about [+5.6, +11.3]%.
findings.fix: In Sec. 3.4 add: 'Set-point residuals are serially correlated (lag-1 r = 0.52 for Ra 80/Ra 20), so the interval understates even the within-mounting uncertainty; allowing for this widens Ra 80 vs Ra 20 to roughly [+7, +21]%.' State that set-point counts are not independent replications. Remove the sign-test sentence, or report it with that caveat.

findings.location: Sec. 5.5, p.11 (and its use in Sec. 7)
findings.quote: Second, n ≈ 3.8 exceeds the aerodynamic n = 3 because the generator dominates it. Fitting Voc ∝ v^1.50 and Rint ∝ v^−0.79 predicts n = 2(1.50) + 0.79 = 3.79 for Ra 20, matching the measurement, so the exponent says little about the blades.
findings.problem: The 'match' is algebraic, not evidence. For a linear V–I ladder Pmax ≈ Voc²/4Rint, so n ≈ 2a − b is guaranteed and says nothing about which component sets the exponent. By the report's own Sec. 5.4 both factors are rotor-side. Voc tracks free-running rotor speed, and its v^1.5 scaling means free-running λ rises with wind (about 0.11 to 0.20), a rotor property (aerodynamics plus fixed friction). The wind-dependent part of Rint is rotor droop ('combines … with the rotor's slowing under load'), because winding resistance does not change with wind. Nothing shown isolates the generator. The claim is also used to wave away what the exponent says about the blades.
findings.evidence: Pmax/(Voc²/4Rint) = 0.94–1.03 at every set point (a1.py), so the identity holds by construction. Voc exponent 1.497 and Rint exponent −0.791 reproduce from Table 9. The July EMF line gives λ_free rising from 0.113 to 0.201 for Ra 20 (a4.py).
findings.fix: Replace with: 'n ≈ 3.8 exceeds 3 because free-running speed rises faster than wind speed (Voc ∝ v^1.5, i.e. λ rising from about 0.11 to 0.20) and the rotor droops less under load at higher wind (Rint ∝ v^−0.79). Both are rotor-side, so the exponent reflects the rotor's speed–wind characteristic, including friction, not the generator alone.' Remove 'the exponent says little about the blades'.

findings.location: Sec. 7 (ii), p.14; Sec. 7 'Mounting and friction', p.15
findings.quote: A constant (Coulomb-type) friction or cut-in difference between rotors would change the exponent (Section 5.5), so it is excluded. A genuine change in the rotor's aerodynamic torque coefficient, or a difference in losses that scale with rotor speed, would both give exactly this signature.
findings.problem: The either/or split is not derived, and it is wrong in kind. Under the report's own scaling, any loss whose power does not scale like the output (∝ v^3.77) changes the exponent, and the difference between loss types is one of degree. A viscous loss (torque ∝ ω) changes it by about −0.06 to −0.10 for the observed gains, which sits at the edge of the Δn intervals, so the data neither cleanly admit it ('exactly this signature') nor cleanly exclude it. Separately, Sec. 7 keeps 'bearing preload' (a constant, Coulomb-type friction) as 'the main open alternative' after (ii) says Coulomb-type differences are excluded. The two statements contradict each other.
findings.evidence: With ω ∝ Voc ∝ v^1.5 and Pmax ∝ v^3.77, a loss torque ∝ ω^p costs power ∝ v^{1.5(p+1)}, so its relative effect ∝ v^{1.5(p+1)−3.77} and Δn ≈ (1.5(p+1) − 3.77)·G, where G is the log gain. Viscous (p = 1): Δn ≈ −0.77G = −0.062 (Ra 40, G = 0.081) and −0.099 (Ra 80, G = 0.128), against CIs [−0.055, +0.061] and [−0.047, +0.095]. Coulomb (p = 0): Δn ≈ −2.27G = −0.18 to −0.29, clearly excluded. The report's own cut-in model sits in between (Δn/G ≈ −1.06).
findings.fix: Rewrite (ii): 'A constant-friction difference large enough to explain the gain would lower n by about 0.2–0.3 and is excluded. Losses that rise with speed (viscous bearing drag, windage, imbalance) would lower n by only about 0.06–0.10, which the present intervals barely resolve. Only a change whose torque scales like the aerodynamic torque leaves n exactly unchanged.' In 'Mounting and friction', drop preload or say that the exponent argues against it, leaving speed-dependent losses open.

findings.location: Sec. 7 'Electrical power is not aerodynamic efficiency', p.15
findings.quote: That limitation is less serious here than usual, because the Thévenin analysis shows the textured rotors spinning faster as well as producing more
findings.problem: This turns the key caveat around. Free-running speed is exactly the quantity that friction, preload and alignment change, and the rotors are compared at different λ. The project's own results page (docs/09) says electrical power can rank rotors 'purely by how freely they spin'. Showing that the textured rotors spin faster unloaded therefore does not reduce the Cp(λ) limitation; it is the confound that limitation is about. At λ ≈ 0.1–0.2 (see above), the measurement also says nothing about Cp near a useful operating point.
findings.evidence: docs/09_results.md: 'a blade that captures more energy but spins slower produces less voltage and therefore reads lower. Two rotors five times apart in aerodynamic efficiency could rank purely by how freely they spin.' The report's own Sec. 5.4 says 'more aerodynamic torque and less parasitic torque would both raise free-running speed'.
findings.fix: Replace with: 'The Thévenin analysis shows the textured rotors spin faster unloaded, but that is exactly what lower parasitic torque would also produce, and the rotors are compared at different tip-speed ratios. It does not substitute for a Cp(λ) comparison, which needs a trustworthy rotor-speed channel.'

findings.location: Sec. 7 'The blade geometry matters', p.15 (vs Sec. 7 (iii), p.14); reference [1]
findings.quote: an aerodynamic one, through texture on the convex back of the returning blade, where separation is not pinned by an edge
findings.problem: The remaining aerodynamic path the report proposes (roughness moving separation on a convex surface to cut drag on the returning blade) is itself a boundary-layer mechanism of the golf-ball kind, which (iii) has just argued against. The discussion dismisses and then adopts the same mechanism. The supporting citation also does not fit: Laitone (1997) tests rectangular wings (flat and lightly cambered plates, NACA 0012) at Re ≤ 7×10^4. The rotor has 183° semicircular buckets at λ ≈ 0.1–0.2 and Re up to 1.2×10^5. Re-insensitivity from edge-fixed separation holds on the concave side of a bucket, not the convex side, as the report's own second path concedes. For a curved bluff surface with k/c ≈ 1–4×10^−3 (0.05–0.2 mm on 48 mm), a roughness-triggered drag crisis near Re ~10^5 lies within the tested range.
findings.evidence: Report text, Sec. 7 (iii) and the 'Two paths remain' bullets. Title and scope of Laitone, Exp. Fluids 23:405–409 (1997) checked via Springer (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s003480050128). The Voc trend for Ra 80 rising with wind speed (see the critical finding on (iii)) is the signature this path predicts.
findings.fix: Merge (iii) and the convex-back bullet: 'The most plausible aerodynamic path is roughness on the convex (returning) side moving separation and reducing drag, a golf-ball-type effect. The rising Ra 80 Voc advantage at higher wind is consistent with it.' Replace [1] with bluff-body or drag-rotor references (drag of semicircular cylinders and cups; roughness on Savonius blades), or limit the Laitone claim to lightly cambered plates.

findings.location: Sec. 6.2, p.13 ('That ratio is not a texture effect'); 'defensible conclusion' paragraph
findings.quote: That ratio is not a texture effect, for three reasons.
findings.problem: The reasons given show only that the ratio cannot be attributed to texture, not that it is not texture. The loading reason covers 900–1300 rpm only. At 1400–1800 rpm the lab's load was 87–94% of the rig's max-power current, so loading costs at most about 2%, yet the ratio there is 0.82–0.91. At face value, on the lab's current scale, the no-texture rotor is below all three textured prints at every loaded set point, in the same direction as the rig's trend. What actually makes the comparison unusable is the current scale. The prior verification found indirect evidence that the lab current may under-read by 10–60%, which could put the no-texture rotor above the textured ones. The report says only that the scale 'cannot be checked from the file'. Taegu Kang and Prof. Jeong will read this paragraph most closely.
findings.evidence: Linear-Thévenin loading correction P/Pmax = 1 − (1 − I/Impp)², using Ra 20 Impp = Voc/2Rint (Table 9) and the lab mean currents (Table 6): I/Impp = 0.88, 0.94, 0.87, 0.92, 0.94 at 1400–1800; loading-corrected ratios 0.90, 0.92, 0.90, 0.89, 0.83. build/audit2/july-verify_details.md: 'Against the rig's V-I curves the lab's voltage is 1.1 V lower at the same labelled current. The rig would need 1.10-1.60× the current.'
findings.fix: Replace with: 'That ratio cannot be read as a texture effect. At 900–1300 rpm the lab's load was below the power maximum. At 1400–1800 rpm loading explains at most 2%, but the lab current scale (2 A/V) is unverified, and a comparison of V–I curves suggests it may under-read by 10–60%, enough to reverse the sign. Window placement also affects 1300–1600 rpm.' Change 'neither clearly above nor clearly below' to 'below the textured prints at face value, but by less than the current-scale uncertainty'.

findings.quote: The June values sit close to the rig's Ra 20 curve (Fig. 8b).
findings.problem: This sentence is the report's only answer to Prof. Jeong's explicit request to compare with the initial test, and it relies on the eye on linear axes, where an 8–14% effect is invisible. Set point by set point, the June table ranges from 0.93× to 1.56× Ra 20 and is 24–25% above Ra 20 at 1200 and 1400 rpm, a spread larger than the whole Ra 20→Ra 80 gap. The June rotor was probably a different one (the report's own inference), and the table uses a different statistic (maxima of 50-sample averages, which still carry some noise bias). 'Close to Ra 20' invites the reading that the original rotor matches Ra 20.
findings.fix: Replace with: 'Set point by set point the June values range from 0.93 to 1.56 times the rig's Ra 20, more than the entire texture effect, and they come from a different rotor and processing, so they cannot place the original rotor relative to the textured prints.'

findings.quote: The open-circuit voltage Voc is the generator EMF with no load, so it is proportional to the rotor's free-running speed. … With no load, the textured rotors spin faster in the same wind
findings.problem: Voc is the intercept of a straight-line fit through loaded dwells, not a no-load measurement, and the relation to speed is affine, not proportional. Across the rectifier the EMF line has a −0.45 V offset. The measured voltage at the lightest step (1 mA) differs from the fitted intercept by −12% at 500 rpm to +3.5% at high wind, so the V–I curve bends near zero current. At 500 rpm the first dwell was taken while the rotor was still spinning up: V rises from the 1 mA to the 2 mA step in all three runs. The ratios survive (first-step voltages agree), but the absolute 'no load / proportional' wording is inaccurate. The offset also makes the Voc percentages slightly overstate the speed change (by about 0.5 point at low wind).
findings.evidence: v_light/Voc: Ra 20 0.895 at 500 rpm, 1.02–1.035 at 1400–1800; similar for Ra 40 and Ra 80 (a1.py). First dwells at 500 rpm: Ra 20 2.848→2.970 V, Ra 40 2.988→3.155 V, Ra 80 2.938→3.084 V at 1→2 mA. July EMF line Voc = 0.03342·rpm − 0.448 V (FINDINGS.md §6).
findings.fix: Write: 'Voc, the zero-current intercept of the fitted line, tracks the generator EMF and hence rotor speed (to within a rectifier offset of about 0.45 V).' Replace the bold sentence with 'At the lightest load the textured rotors' terminal voltage is higher, so they spin faster in the same wind.' Note that the 500 rpm first dwell is not settled.

findings.quote: The Voc change alone accounts for 92% and 97% of the power gain.
findings.problem: The precision is spurious, and the base is unstated. The share is 2Δln Voc/(2Δln Voc − Δln Rint), a share of the modelled gain, not of the measured Pmax gain. Because the Rint change is indistinguishable from zero, the share's uncertainty spans 100%.
findings.evidence: a2.py. Bootstrap 95% ranges for the share: Ra 40 0.74–1.14, Ra 80 0.86–1.11; at the Rint CI ends 0.75–1.21 and 0.85–1.14. 2Δln Voc against the measured Δln Pmax: 0.0800/0.0808 = 0.99 (Ra 40), 0.1242/0.1287 = 0.96 (Ra 80).
findings.fix: Replace with: 'Within its uncertainty, the Voc change accounts for all of the power gain (point estimates 92% and 97%, each ±about 15–20%).'

findings.quote: Power scales with air density; day-to-day density changes in an indoor laboratory are a few percent at most, smaller than the observed differences but not negligible against them.
findings.problem: This assumes Pmax ∝ ρ. On this rig Pmax rises with dynamic pressure much faster than linearly (n = 3.77, i.e. ∝ q^1.9 through wind speed), and a density change acts partly like a change in dynamic pressure. Sensitivity to ρ could therefore be anywhere from about 1 to about 1.9. A 2–3% density difference could move Pmax by up to about 4–6%, the size of the Ra 80 vs Ra 40 step (+4.9%), so 'smaller than the observed differences' is not safe for that contrast.
findings.evidence: Power-law exponents in Table 5 (3.76–3.79). Ra 40 is the only run with ambient data, from an uncalibrated sensor (header note: 'reads ~20 C high when it has been powered a while').
findings.fix: 'Density differences of a few percent could change Pmax by up to about twice that on this rig, comparable to the Ra 80 vs Ra 40 difference; calibrated ambient logging on every run is needed.'
